items.alt: A stack of machined aluminum Lego 2x4 bricks
Top view of machined aluminum Lego 2x4 bricks
Bottom view of machined aluminum Lego 2x4 bricks

content.html: I machined these Lego 2x4 bricks to practice precision with multiple tool and multiple setup parts before teaching my class at Artisan's Asylum on the CNC mill. The original CAD file is taken from LeoCAD and matches exactly the specified dimensions of a Lego 2x4 Brick. The bricks were milled in two setups. Firstly, rough cut 6061 stock was held in dovetail vise jaws. The outline of the brick and bottom face were cut with a 1/2" end mill. After that, 1/8", 3/32", and finally 0.040" endmills were used to clear out the bottom cavity of the brick. After this, the brick was turned over and placed on parallels in the vise. The top face was cut with the 1/2" end mill, and the 1/8" and 3/32" end mills were used to contour the studs. The final brick is of sufficiently high tolerance to achieve an interference fit with real ABS Lego bricks. All dimensions are to within +0mm -0.1mm. There is a slight misalignment of less than 0.05mm, as measured with a surface plate and feeler gauges, between the top and bottom setups. This is likely due to the lack of rigidity in the endstop that I used to locate the bricks in the second setup. If I were top do these again I would probably create some type of purpose-built fixture to locate the parts more precisely for the second setup.

items.alt: A completed CNC mill class hexagonal machined part

content.html: This is the part that my students make in my Introduction to CNC Milling class at Artisan's Asylum. In the first session of the class, they go over basic machine operation and setup by squaring up a rectangular piece of stock. In the second, they go over work coordinate systems and offsets by drilling holes in the rectangular block. In the third session, they copy this part. We cover offsets and tool changes for using multiple tools in one part, CAM for operations including facing, 2d contouring, 3d surfacing and text engraving, and aligning a part through multiple workholding setups. The part starts off with 1.5" hex bar stock rough sawn to length. The operations involved begin with facing the stock and then cutting the lower and upper steps of the hexagon with 2d contours using a 1/2" endmill. Next, they move on to cutting fillet with a 3d surfacing operation using a 1/4" ball endmill. Then they move on to engraving the text using a 1/8" 30 degree vee engraving cutter. The final operation is to remove the part from the vise, flip it over and redo the offsets, and face off the remainder of the rough stock from the bottom of the part. This is the example that I completed myself for the students to use as a reference. All the hexagonal faces are within +0.002" -0.000" of the drawing spec.

items.title: Embedded C++ 3D Rendering Engine Demo
items.allow: accelerometer; autoplay; clipboard-write; encrypted-media; gyroscope; picture-in-picture; web-share

content.html: I wrote this 3D renderer from scratch as a part of an interactive art project that I have not yet finished. I wrote it entirely from scratch, using only a framebuffer object with pixel and triangle draw functionality for output and matrices for calculating the transforms. The renderer uses triangle meshes and supports rotation, scaling, and translation. Flat shading is implemented with ambient and directional lighting in an 8-bit color space. In order to generate the the shape data I wrote a Python script to convert .OBJ files to a struct in the format I specified for the renderer. Performance is limited to 29 frames per second due to the maximum throughput of the screen data interface, but for a 60-polygon shape the theroetical performance with lighting could be up to 800 FPS. I had originally learned the relevant math in an undergraduate class on computer graphics, and this was an interesting way to revisit one of my favorite courses several years later. The larger project will integrate a variety of interactive controls to change different parameters about the polyhedron and its animation.

items.title: CR10-S 3D Printer Digital Twin Demo
items.allow: accelerometer; autoplay; clipboard-write; encrypted-media; gyroscope; picture-in-picture; web-share

content.html: For a class in the spring 2026 semester, I implemented a fully integrated, live state-synchronized digital twin of my 3D printer. This system allows real-time, spatially accurate remote visualization of the printer as it is running. The printer is a modified Creality CR10-S with a BTT Octopus Pro motherboard and an ESP32 installed in an expansion header. The printer is setup to emit telemetry of position and temperatures on its serial ports at a rate of 1Hz through M154/M155. The ESP32 is connected to one of the motherboard's serial ports, and exposes a telnet connection on the local network. A Python script running on another machine connects to the ESP32, receives and parses the telemetry, and publishes it in formatted JSON to an MQTT broker. The digital twin itself runs in a Unity app on a PC. The Unity app connects to the MQTT broker and subscribes to the telemetry topics. The incoming telemetry is then used to move the digital printer geometry to match the position of the real printer. Temperature telemetry is used to calculate deviation from programmed temperature for both the bed and extruder, which is represented by changing the material color of each respectively. The position of the extruder is tracked with a series of colored dots, which over the course of the print build up the shape of the printed object. The digital twin can also publish G-code commands to the broker, which are subscribed by the Python script and then passed on to the ESP32 and subsequently to the printer.

items.alt: A 2/3 scale replica of a historic stained glass window

content.html: I grew up in a house that used to be a church rectory, and in the hallway outside my room there is a beautiful 100 year old stained glass window. As an anniversary gift to my parents, I created a 2/3 scale replica of it. The panes are pearlescent acrylic, and the designs in the dark blue panes were etched with a laser cutter and filled with gold enamel paint. The glazing is made of laser-cut plywood and stained with translucent food dye to give a nice color without overwhelming the grain of the top veneer. The frame is made of oak trim salvaged during renovations in the same house. When held up to the light, the colors almost match the original.

items.alt: A brass butterfly brooch with geometric lattice wings

content.html: For my last high school reunion, there was a black tie dinner. I had worn a tux exactly twice before, for my junior and senior proms, and the same one was hanging in my closet. On the last occasion I had worn a brooch of a butterfly instead of a traditional boutonniere. That one was long gone, but it was a nice starting point for a unique new item of jewelry. In Onshape I imported a photo of a blue Ulysses butterfly and traced the outline in a relatively blocky shape. I then freehanded a lattice of cells inside the wings in a pattern evocative of the real thing but stylized with sharp angles. I was lucky enough to have access to a waterjet cutter, and using an eye-wateringly expensive amount of garnet I cut the shape out of a sheet of 1/16th inch brass. I wire brushed it to a shiny finish and screwed it to a binder clip for a hanger.

items.alt: A 1986 VDO tachometer converted into a clock

content.html: My father is a big fan of vintage German cars. I was searching for something Porsche-themed to get him for Christmas a few years ago when I came across this tachometer from a 1986 Mercedes S-class. I immediately thought it would make a great clock face, given that it redlines at 60 and already has a clock. I hooked it up to 12v which takes care of the hour and minute hand. For the second hand, I connected the tachometer input through a level shifter to a PWM pin on a microcontroller. By sweeping the frequency from 0-750Hz (8-cylinder engine) over the course of a minute, I got it to glide smoothly from 0-60.

projects.title: Digital Horn With Flight Stick Shift

items.alt: A fabricated flight stick shift knob installed in a WRX
The custom electronics and horn controls built into the flight stick shifter

content.html: My second car was a 2010 WRX. I loved it, and while I wanted to keep the mechanicals completely stock, I wanted to add something personal to it. I started off with a flight stick controller thinking it could just be a cool shift knob. Once I started fabricating it, I thought that the buttons might have another use. I squeezed an IO expander inside the handle and connected it to the controller's original buttons. Using shielded cable with aviation connectors and a low clock speed, I was able to get the I2C connection working even over 1 meter of cable in the noisy environment of a car. Using a Pi Pico, I read the buttons from the flight stick and used them to trigger audio files from an SD card on a serial-controlled MP3 module. I then boxed that up with an amplifier and wired it to a speaker right next to the car's original horn. With the press of a few buttons, the car now had a vintage klaxon and la cucaracha as well as the regular horn blast.

items.alt: A vintage Yellow Springs Instruments thermometer converted into a weather station

content.html: One of my favorite places to start with a project is a vintage device. I love looking at old instruments and electronics and imagining what else it could be. The cases were made better, with more space, more metal, and less thin plastic. The controls and displays are beautifully analog. In the case of this Yellow Springs Instruments lab thermometer, the large temperature gauge makes a perfect display for a weather station. The gauge is a DC current meter with an approximate range of 5ma. The original thermometer circuit was quite simple, just a wheatstone bridge with a D battery as a voltage source used to read a thermistor temperature probe. After gutting the original board, I installed a new driver for the gauge and knob. The core is a Pico W, which reads the current temperature and humidity in Boston from the NOAA weather API. For indoor measurements, I fitted a DHT11 to the front of the case. The knob allows selection between displaying the outdoor temperature, outdoor humidity, indoor temperature, and indoor humidity. As the Fahrenheit scale only goes down to 40 on the low end, I needed to use the Celsius scale for measurements lower than this. The blue LED indicates when the number should be read off the lower scale. The white LED indicates if there is rain or snow in the day's forecast. To drive the gauge, I simply connected it through a resistor-capacitor network to a digital pin, and drove it with a PWM signal to generate a variable current. In order to pin the gauge to the low end of the scale, it actually requires a slight negative current. I used a potentiometer as a voltage divider to provide a non-zero reference for the <q>ground</q> end of the gauge, creating negative current when the pin is driven at 0% duty.

items.title: Antikythera Mechanism Replica Demo
items.allow: accelerometer; autoplay; clipboard-write; encrypted-media; gyroscope; picture-in-picture; web-share

items.alt: The front of the completed mechanism

content.html: In spring 2023, I was assigned in a history class to research an ancient technology and produce a replica of it. I selected the antikythera mechanism, an ancient greek mechanical computer used to calculate the cycles of various astronomical objects. I decided that my replica would be somewhat simplified, calculating only the cycles of the sun and moon through one metonic cycle. After calculating the necessary ratios, I designed a geartrain in Onshape that would move the pointers appropriately, then cut the backplate and all the gears on a CNC waterjet cutter.

items.alt: The antikythera mechanism open in Onshape
The final assembled mechanism, turned to show the gears

content.html: I turned the pins manually on a lathe. A classmate drew a beatiful decoration, which we scanned and etched onto the plate using laser marking fluid. The final result works very well, and is accurate to within one lunar month through a 19-solar year metonic cycle. (It could be made more accurate by using precut gears, but that was over budget for this project unfortunately.) All my CAD work for this project can be viewed in the public Onshape document.

items.alt: The gear indicator in the RPM gauge showing neutral
The gear indicator level shifter board

content.html: This is a gear indicator for my 2006 Suzuki V-Strom DL650. I had seen several versions of this on the internet, but they all used an ELM327. As the motorcycle is quite old, the diagnostic port uses K-Line instead of CANBus/OBDII, which is just a half-duplex UART. I interfaced this to the hardware serial port of an Arduino through a level shifter, and this allowed the Arduino to read the engine diagnostic port directly. For a display solution I put an I2C OLED display in the RPM gauge. Code and circuit diagrams are available on github.

content.html: This is a project I did over summer 2020 for a BU CS200 class taugh by XRTerra, with 2 classmates. We used the unity game engine to make the simulator, and most of the assets and all the scripting are done from scratch. I made all of the assets as well as some of the scripting and physics.You can download the latest build as well as source code on my github.

In 2022, RICM began sponsoring several Rhode Island high schools in establishing a Greenpower F24 electric gokart racing league. The primary purpose of the project is to give the students hands-on practice with fabrication, electronics, and mechanical engineering. The Greenpower foundation used to provide a telemetry kit which measured important statsitics about the car, but as it was very expensive and not available in the US, the museum asked me to design a replacement. Using the original kit as a guide for requirements, I selected parts, designed and ordered a board, and assembled a prototype kit. The kit measures car telemetry statistics like battery level, motor current consumption, motor temperature, and acceleration. We also added additional hardware to display statistics to the driver, and to log data to an SD card for the students to use in redesigning the car.

items.alt: A black 1972 Honda CB350F, heavily modified in the cafe racer style.

content.html: My father bought this motorcycle in 2014, but for the most part it sat in the shed, and when I pulled it out in summer 2023 it had not run in 4 years. It was in pretty decent shape, with the mods halfway to where I wanted it, but the cafe racer bars and seat were very uncomfortable and the carbs and some electrics needed an overhaul. I fully disassembled and rebuilt the carbs, fixing the jetting for the individual velocity stack intakes that replace the stock airbox. After that I swapped the bars for a more comfortable vintage buckhorn handlebar from a BSA. This also meant swapping the brake line, grips, and hand controls. I selected a new seat that kept with the cafe racer style but is much more comfortable and padded, and fabricated a mounting bracket setup on the water jet cutter. I also cut a new dashboard on the waterjet and replaced the indicator lights with a new matching set. It turned out very clean, with nothing unnecessary remaining but keeping true to the vintage cafe racer style.

Over the summer of 2021, Dan Berman, curator at the Rhode Island Computer Museum, asked me to design a new kit for use in the Museum's "learn electronics" workshops for elementary-school children. After thinking about what hardware might be interesting for the project, I settled on a Raspberry Pi Pico, because of its low cost and the ability to program natively in Python. Mike Thompson and I then designed and laid out a circuit board for the hardware I had selected, and we were able to construct several of the kits. The latest iteration costs only $20 for all components and the PCB, allowing us to provide the kit for workshops. Thanks to Dan Berman and RICM for funding the project and Mike Thompson for teaching me how to lay out boards.
